newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown set for further battle as CNB relaxes.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown set for further battle as CNB relaxes.

text.p: Downward pressure on the Czech crown has subsided following a series of Czech National Bank (CNB) moves, but analysts warned on Tuesday that another attack on the currency is likely as the CNB measures are eased.

After months of rock-solid stability, the crown came under fire last week from short-selling, especially by foreign investors, that pushed it to record lows of more than five percent below its basket parity, prompting the CNB to intervene for the first time in more than a year.
The CNB said the crown's fall was due to fluctuations of several foreign currencies and not for fundamental reasons, adding that the bearish pressure has subsided this week.
But analysts said they expect another attack on the crown to begin once the central bank begins to loosen its grip, regardless of the reason behind the first attempt.
"What tends to happen in situations like this is that you get a second attack...and I think you have to expect that," said Pavel Pinkava, a London-based currency dealer at Nomura International.

Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka in Prague agreed: "The CNB showed a strong commitment to keep the crown at current levels. (But) similar attacks (on the crown) look quite probable for the future."
The crown was steady at around 2.0 percent below parity of the central bank's mark/dollar basket in Tuesday afternoon trading from -3.8 percent on Friday.

In an attempt to ward off bearish investors, the central bank last Friday raised its Lombard rate to 50 percent from a previous 14 percent, and followed up with a rise in repo rates to 45 percent from 12.9 percent.
Analysts said the moves may have cost the central bank as much as $1 billion, but they appeared to have had their desired effect. Banks have raised rates and the crown has moved closer to parity.
If the central bank continued to stand its ground, it should win the war and beat back the tide of weaker crown sentiment, analysts said.
"The CNB has got to stand tough right now. It is under government pressure over the economy but if it holds on, it can withstand another wave and win this battle," said one local dealer.

"Over the next couple of weeks, the market will be pretty quiet, and then there will be a final attack, which I think will resolve itself in favour of the central bank, and then they (investors) will walk away," he added.
Nomura's Pinkava agreed. He said the central bank would have to hold rates at current levels for two to three weeks, but that in the end, the central bank should come out on top.

"At the end of the day, these crises often resolve themselves in favour of the central bank, especially the first few times investors attack and especially in this market which isn't that deep," he said.
